title: Maths & Logic
blurb: Numbers, chance, shapes, statistics and clear thinking.

cards.title: The invention of zero
cards.text: Zero as a number, not just a gap, was developed in India; Brahmagupta wrote rules for it around 628 CE. It reached Europe through Arabic scholars, with Hindu-Arabic numerals.

cards.title: Place value
cards.text: In 352, the 3 means three hundreds because of its place. Roman numerals had no place value, which made arithmetic painful: try CCCLII × XLVII.

cards.title: Pi
cards.text: π is the ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter: about 3.14159. Its digits never end or repeat. Archimedes estimated it around 250 BCE.

cards.title: Prime numbers
cards.text: A prime has exactly two divisors: 1 and itself. 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13… Euclid proved around 300 BCE that there are infinitely many.

cards.title: Primes protect your data
cards.text: Multiplying two huge primes is easy; working backwards to find them is extremely hard. RSA encryption, used online, relies on that.

cards.title: The Fibonacci sequence
cards.text: Each number is the sum of the two before it: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21… It appears in sunflower seed spirals and pine cones.

cards.title: Square numbers
cards.text: Square numbers come from multiplying a number by itself: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25. Odd numbers add up to them: 1 + 3 + 5 = 9.

cards.title: Infinity
cards.text: Some infinities are bigger than others. Georg Cantor showed there are more real numbers (all decimals) than whole numbers, even though both are infinite.

cards.title: Negative numbers
cards.text: Negative numbers were used in China over 2,000 years ago for debts. Europeans resisted them until the 1600s. Today they're on every thermometer and bank statement.

cards.title: A trick with 9
cards.text: Multiply 9 by any number from 1 to 10 and the digits of the answer add up to 9: 9 × 7 = 63, and 6 + 3 = 9.

quiz.q: Which of these is a prime number?
What is π?
What comes next: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, …?

cards.title: Probability basics
cards.text: Probability is a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). A fair coin landing heads is 1/2; rolling a six is 1/6.

cards.title: And and or
cards.text: For independent events, multiply for "and": two heads = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. Add for "either", if they can't both happen: a 1 or a 2 on a die = 2/6.

cards.title: The gambler's fallacy

items.w: "Red came up 5 times, black is due"
items.r: Each spin is independent: same odds

cards.text: After five heads in a row, tails isn't "due". Coins have no memory; the next flip is still 50/50.

cards.title: The birthday paradox
cards.text: In a group of just 23 people, there's a better than 50% chance two share a birthday. With 70 people, it's over 99.9%.

cards.title: Expected value
cards.text: Multiply each outcome by its probability and add. A lottery ticket costing €2 with an expected payout of €1 loses €1 on average.

cards.title: Lotteries
cards.text: EuroMillions jackpot odds are about 1 in 140 million. You're far more likely to be struck by lightning in your lifetime.

cards.title: The Monty Hall problem
cards.text: Pick one of three doors; the host, who knows, opens a losing door and offers a switch. Switching wins 2/3 of the time. Even mathematicians got it wrong at first.

cards.title: Base rates
cards.text: A test is 99% accurate for a disease affecting 1 in 1,000 people. If you test positive, the chance you have it is only about 9%, because false positives from healthy people outnumber true cases.

cards.title: Law of large numbers
cards.text: Over a few flips, results can be lopsided. Over thousands, the share of heads gets very close to 50%. Casinos rely on this.

cards.title: Risk in perspective
cards.text: "Doubles the risk" sounds scary, but from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000 is a tiny absolute change. Always ask: out of how many?

quiz.q: After 5 heads in a row, the next flip is…
In the Monty Hall problem, switching wins…
How many people make a shared birthday more likely than not?

cards.title: Pythagoras' theorem
cards.text: In a right-angled triangle, the square on the longest side equals the sum of the squares on the other two. Builders used 3-4-5 triangles to make square corners.

cards.title: The 3-4-5 triangle
cards.text: Measure 3 m along one wall and 4 m along the other. If the diagonal is exactly 5 m, the corner is a perfect right angle.

cards.title: Angles in a triangle
cards.text: The angles in any triangle add up to 180°. Those in a four-sided shape add up to 360°.

cards.title: Area of a circle
cards.text: A circle's area is π times the radius squared. Doubling the radius makes the area four times bigger: why a 40 cm pizza is more than one and a half 30 cm pizzas.

cards.title: Hexagons in nature
cards.text: Bees build hexagonal cells because hexagons tile a surface with no gaps using the least wall material for the area enclosed.

cards.title: Platonic solids
cards.text: Only five solids have identical regular faces with the same number meeting at each corner: tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron. Dice use them.

cards.title: Symmetry
cards.text: A shape has symmetry if a move, such as a reflection or rotation, leaves it looking the same. Snowflakes have six-fold symmetry; your face is roughly mirror-symmetric.

cards.title: Scaling
cards.text: If you double the size of an object, its area grows four times and its volume eight times. That's why giant insects couldn't hold themselves up.

cards.title: Map projections
cards.text: You can't flatten a sphere without distortion. The Mercator map keeps angles right for navigation but makes Greenland look as big as Africa, which is about 14 times larger.

cards.title: Fractals
cards.text: Fractals repeat their pattern at every scale: coastlines, ferns, broccoli and lightning. Zoom in and you see the same shape again.

quiz.q: What's the hypotenuse of a triangle with sides 3 and 4?
Double the size of a cube: its volume grows…

cards.title: Mean, median, mode
cards.text: The mean is the average; the median is the middle value; the mode is the most common. They can differ a lot.

cards.title: When the mean misleads
cards.text: If a billionaire walks into a café, the mean wealth of the customers shoots up, but the median barely moves. Salaries are better described by the median.

cards.title: Spread
cards.text: Two classes can have the same average but very different spreads. The standard deviation measures how far values typically are from the mean.

cards.title: The bell curve
cards.text: Many measurements, like heights, cluster around an average in a bell shape. About 68% of values fall within one standard deviation and 95% within two.

cards.title: Samples
cards.text: A well-chosen random sample of 1,000 people can represent millions. A big but biased sample can't: who you ask matters more than how many.

cards.title: Margin of error
cards.text: Polls report a margin of error. With about 1,000 people it's roughly ±3 percentage points, so 51% vs 49% may be a tie.

cards.title: Misleading charts

items.r: Check the axis: it's a 2% difference

cards.text: A chart's y-axis that doesn't start at zero can make a small difference look huge. Always check the scale.

cards.title: Simpson's paradox
cards.text: A trend in every group can reverse when the groups are combined. A treatment can look better in each hospital but worse overall, if hospitals have different patient mixes.

cards.title: Regression to the mean
cards.text: After an extreme result, the next tends to be closer to average. A sports star's record season is often followed by a more ordinary one, without any curse.

cards.title: Reading a news statistic
cards.text: Ask four questions: compared with what? Out of how many? Who was measured? Who paid for the study?

quiz.q: Which average is best for describing typical salaries?
quiz.explain: A few very high earners pull the mean up.

quiz.q: About what share of values fall within 1 standard deviation in a bell curve?

lessons.title: Logic and puzzles
lessons.summary: Clear thinking, from paradoxes to computers.

cards.title: True and false

items.b: true if at least one true

cards.text: Logic works with statements that are true or false and combines them with AND, OR and NOT. Every computer chip is built from these operations.

cards.title: If… then…

items.r: Something else could have wet it

cards.text: "If it rains, the ground is wet" doesn't mean "if the ground is wet, it rained": a sprinkler could do that. Confusing the two is a classic logic error.

cards.title: Proof by contradiction
cards.text: Assume the opposite of what you want to prove and show it leads to nonsense. Euclid proved infinitely many primes this way.

cards.title: The liar paradox
cards.text: "This sentence is false." If it's true, it's false; if it's false, it's true. Paradoxes like this shook the foundations of logic in the 20th century.

cards.title: Gödel's incompleteness
cards.text: In 1931 Kurt Gödel proved that any consistent system of rules rich enough for arithmetic has true statements it can't prove. Mathematics can never be complete.

cards.title: Algorithms
cards.text: An algorithm is a precise step-by-step recipe for solving a problem. The word comes from the name of al-Khwarizmi, a 9th-century mathematician in Baghdad.

cards.title: Binary
cards.text: Computers count in base 2, using only 0 and 1. Each place is worth double the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16…

cards.title: Zeno's paradox
cards.text: To cross a room, you must first cross half, then half of what's left, forever. Zeno said you'd never arrive. The infinite sum 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … actually equals 1.

cards.title: Unsolved problems
cards.text: Some simple-sounding questions remain unsolved, like Goldbach's conjecture: is every even number above 2 the sum of two primes? Tested to huge numbers, never proved.

cards.title: The river crossing
cards.text: A farmer must cross a river with a wolf, a goat and a cabbage, taking one at a time. The wolf can't be left with the goat, nor the goat with the cabbage. The trick: bring the goat back.

quiz.q: What is 101 in binary as a normal number?
"If it rains, the ground is wet. The ground is wet." Does it follow that it rained?
quiz.explain: Something else could have wet it.

cards.title: What a percentage is
cards.text: "Per cent" means "out of 100". 25% is 25 out of 100, or a quarter. To find a percentage of a number, multiply by the percentage and divide by 100.

cards.title: Quick tricks
cards.text: 10% is easy: move the decimal point one place left. From there, 5% is half of that and 20% is double.

cards.title: Percentages flip
cards.text: 8% of 25 equals 25% of 8, because multiplication works both ways. Use whichever is easier: 4% of 75 is 75% of 4, which is 3.

cards.title: Up then down
cards.text: A 50% rise followed by a 50% fall doesn't return you to the start. €100 becomes €150, then €75.

cards.title: Percentage points
cards.text: If interest rates go from 2% to 3%, that's a rise of 1 percentage point, but a 50% increase in the rate. Headlines often mix them up.

cards.title: Reverse percentages
cards.text: A price including 23% VAT is €123. The price before VAT isn't €123 minus 23%; it's €123 ÷ 1.23 = €100.

cards.title: Discounts stack strangely
cards.text: "30% off, plus an extra 20% off" is not 50% off. It's 0.7 × 0.8 = 0.56 of the price: a 44% discount.

cards.title: Percentage change
cards.text: Change ÷ original × 100. From 80 to 100 is a 25% rise; from 100 back to 80 is a 20% fall. The starting point matters.

cards.title: Tips and splits
cards.text: To split a €60 bill with a 10% tip among four: €60 × 1.1 = €66, divided by 4 = €16.50 each.

cards.title: Misleading percentages
cards.text: "Sales up 200%!" from 1 to 3 units sounds dramatic but means little. Always ask for the actual numbers behind a percentage.

quiz.q: A €100 item rises 50%, then falls 50%. What does it cost?
A price with 23% VAT is €123. What's the price without VAT?
"30% off then 20% off" equals a discount of…

cards.title: Fractions are division
cards.text: 3/4 means 3 divided by 4: three of four equal parts, or 0.75. The bottom number says how many parts; the top says how many you take.

cards.title: Equivalent fractions
cards.text: Multiplying top and bottom by the same number doesn't change a fraction: 1/2 = 2/4 = 50/100. Simplify by dividing both by a common factor.

cards.title: Adding fractions
cards.text: To add fractions, give them the same bottom number first: 1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.

cards.title: Multiplying fractions
cards.text: Multiply tops together and bottoms together. Half of three-quarters is 1/2 × 3/4 = 3/8. "Of" means multiply.

cards.title: Dividing by a fraction

items.r: 3 ÷ ½ = 6, since six halves make three

cards.text: Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its flip. 3 ÷ 1/2 = 6: how many halves fit in 3? Six.

cards.title: Ratios
cards.text: A ratio compares quantities. A 2:3 mix of cement to sand means 2 parts cement for every 3 of sand: 2/5 of the mix is cement.

cards.title: Scaling recipes
cards.text: A recipe for 4 needs 300 g of flour. For 6 people, multiply by 6/4 = 1.5: 450 g.

cards.title: Unit rates
cards.text: Compare deals by price per unit. 500 g for €2.40 is €4.80/kg; 750 g for €3.30 is €4.40/kg. The bigger pack is cheaper here, but not always.

cards.title: Map scales
cards.text: On a 1:25,000 map, 1 cm is 25,000 cm, which is 250 m on the ground. Hiking maps often use this scale.

cards.title: Direct and inverse proportion
cards.text: Twice the hours at the same pay means twice the money: direct proportion. Twice the workers on a job means half the time: inverse proportion, roughly.

quiz.q: What is 1/2 + 1/3?
What is 3 ÷ ½?
quiz.explain: How many halves fit in three?

cards.title: Round and adjust
cards.text: To add 298 + 157, add 300 and take away 2: 457 − 2 = 455. Rounding to friendly numbers makes many sums easy.

cards.title: Multiply by 5
cards.text: To multiply by 5, multiply by 10 and halve. 5 × 48 = 480 ÷ 2 = 240.

cards.title: Multiply by 11
cards.text: For a two-digit number, add the digits and put the sum in the middle: 11 × 36 = 3(3+6)6 = 396. If the sum is 10 or more, carry one.

cards.title: Squares ending in 5
cards.text: To square a number ending in 5, multiply the first part by the next number up and stick 25 on the end: 35² = (3 × 4) then 25 = 1,225.

cards.title: Doubling and halving
cards.text: Halve one number and double the other: the product stays the same. 16 × 25 = 8 × 50 = 4 × 100 = 400.

cards.title: Break it apart
cards.text: Split awkward multiplications: 7 × 48 = 7 × 50 − 7 × 2 = 350 − 14 = 336.

cards.title: Divisibility tests
cards.text: A number divides by 3 if its digits add up to a multiple of 3; by 9 if they add up to a multiple of 9; by 4 if its last two digits do.

cards.title: Estimate first
cards.text: Before calculating, estimate. 49 × 21 is about 50 × 20 = 1,000; if your answer is 10,290, something went wrong.

cards.title: Counting up for change
cards.text: Shopkeepers give change by counting up. Paying €20 for €13.65: up to €14 is 35 cents, up to €20 is €6, so €6.35.

cards.title: Converting temperatures
cards.text: Rough Celsius to Fahrenheit: double and add 30. 20 °C ≈ 70 °F (exactly 68). For the exact value, multiply by 1.8 and add 32.

quiz.q: What is 11 × 43?
What is 45²?

cards.title: What algebra is
cards.text: Algebra uses letters for numbers we don't know yet. "A number plus 5 is 12" becomes x + 5 = 12, so x = 7.

cards.title: Keep it balanced
cards.text: An equation is a balance: whatever you do to one side, do to the other. Subtract 5 from both sides of x + 5 = 12 to get x = 7.

cards.title: Two-step equations
cards.text: 3x + 4 = 19: subtract 4 from both sides (3x = 15), then divide both by 3 (x = 5). Undo operations in reverse order.

cards.title: Where it came from
cards.text: The word "algebra" comes from *al-jabr*, "restoring", in the title of al-Khwarizmi's 9th-century book in Baghdad. Letters for unknowns came later, with François Viète in the 1590s.

cards.title: Formulas are algebra
cards.text: Every formula is algebra: area = length × width, speed = distance ÷ time. Rearranging lets you find any missing piece.

cards.title: Expanding brackets
cards.text: Multiply everything inside by what's outside: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12. Handy for mental maths too: 3 × 104 = 300 + 12.

cards.title: Two unknowns
cards.text: Two coffees and a cake cost €5; one coffee and a cake cost €3.50. Subtract: one coffee is €1.50, so the cake is €2. That's a system of equations.

cards.title: Negative signs
cards.text: Subtracting a negative is adding: 5 − (−3) = 8. Multiplying two negatives gives a positive: (−2) × (−3) = 6.

cards.title: Sequences as formulas
cards.text: In 3, 5, 7, 9…, each term is 2n + 1. Find the 100th term without listing: 2 × 100 + 1 = 201.

cards.title: A real problem
cards.text: A phone plan costs €10 a month plus €0.05 per MB. With €15 a month, how many MB? 10 + 0.05m = 15, so m = 100 MB.

quiz.q: Solve 3x + 4 = 19.
What is 5 − (−3)?

cards.title: Linear vs exponential
cards.text: Linear growth adds the same amount each step; exponential growth multiplies. Exponential starts slow and then explodes.

cards.title: The chessboard legend
cards.text: Put 1 grain of rice on the first square, 2 on the next, 4, 8… By square 64, you'd need about 18 quintillion grains, far more than all rice ever grown.

cards.title: The lily pond
cards.text: Lilies double daily and cover a pond on day 30. When was it half covered? Day 29. Exponential problems look small until the very end.

cards.title: Powers
cards.text: 2⁵ means 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32. Powers are a shorthand for repeated multiplication. Any number to the power 0 is 1.

cards.title: Logarithms
cards.text: A logarithm asks: "what power?" log₁₀ 1,000 = 3, because 10³ = 1,000. Logs turn huge multiplications into simple additions.

cards.title: Log scales around us
cards.text: The Richter-type earthquake scale, decibels and pH all use logs. Each step up in magnitude means about 32 times more energy released.

cards.title: Viruses spread
cards.text: If each infected person infects 2 others every few days, cases double. Bringing that number below 1 makes an epidemic shrink.

cards.title: Moore's law
cards.text: Gordon Moore noticed in 1965 that the number of transistors on chips doubled about every two years. It held for decades, powering the digital revolution.

cards.title: Half-life
cards.text: Radioactive substances decay exponentially. After one half-life, half remains; after two, a quarter. Carbon-14's half-life of 5,730 years lets us date ancient remains.

cards.title: Paper folding
cards.text: A sheet of paper about 0.1 mm thick folded 42 times would be over 400,000 km thick, past the Moon. In practice, you can't fold paper more than about 7 times by hand.

quiz.q: A pond is fully covered on day 30, doubling daily. When was it half covered?
What is log₁₀ 1,000?

cards.title: What a function is
cards.text: A function is a rule that turns each input into exactly one output, like a machine: put in 3, the rule "double it" gives 6.

cards.title: Coordinates
cards.text: Descartes' idea: describe any point by two numbers, (x, y): how far across and how far up. It joined algebra and geometry.

cards.title: Straight lines
cards.text: y = mx + c draws a straight line: m is the slope (how steep), c is where it crosses the y-axis.

cards.title: A taxi fare
cards.text: A taxi charges €3.50 to start plus €1.20 per km. Fare = 1.2 × km + 3.5: a straight line. 10 km costs €15.50.

cards.title: Slope means rate
cards.text: The slope is a rate of change: euros per km, km per hour, degrees per minute. Steeper lines mean faster change.

cards.title: Curves
cards.text: y = x² makes a U-shaped curve called a parabola. A ball thrown in the air follows one, and satellite dishes use its shape to focus signals.

cards.title: Reading graphs

items: Does the axis start at zero?

cards.text: Before reading a graph, check what each axis shows, the units and the scale. Then look at the overall shape before the details.

cards.title: Shapes of change
cards.text: Lines show steady change; upward curves show acceleration; curves that level off show saturation, like a phone battery charging.

cards.title: Inverse relationships
cards.text: Some quantities move in opposite directions: travel time falls as speed rises. The graph curves down without ever reaching zero.

cards.title: Functions in code
cards.text: Spreadsheets and programs are full of functions: =SUM(), =AVERAGE(). Each takes inputs and returns one output, exactly like the maths.

quiz.q: In y = mx + c, what does m tell you?
What shape does y = x² make?
On a distance–time graph, the slope shows…

cards.title: What game theory studies
cards.text: Game theory studies decisions where your best choice depends on what others do: business, politics, biology, even crossing the road.

cards.title: The prisoner's dilemma
cards.text: Two suspects can stay silent or betray each other. Betraying is better for each individually, yet if both betray, both end up worse off than if both had stayed silent.

cards.title: Nash equilibrium
cards.text: A Nash equilibrium is a situation where nobody gains by changing their choice alone. John Nash, subject of *A Beautiful Mind*, defined it in 1950.

cards.title: Repeated games
cards.text: When the game repeats, cooperation can win. In Robert Axelrod's 1980s computer tournaments, "tit for tat" (cooperate first, then copy the other) did remarkably well.

cards.title: Zero-sum games
cards.text: In zero-sum games, one player's gain is exactly the other's loss, like poker or chess. Most of life, including trade, isn't zero-sum: both sides can gain.

cards.title: Chicken
cards.text: Two drivers speed towards each other; whoever swerves loses face, but if neither swerves, both crash. It models stand-offs between countries or companies.

cards.title: First-mover advantage
cards.text: In some games, moving first lets you commit and shape the outcome. In others, waiting lets you learn from the leader's mistakes.

cards.title: Auctions
cards.text: Game theory designs auctions for radio spectrum worth billions. In a sealed second-price auction, the best strategy is to bid exactly what it's worth to you.

cards.title: Evolution as a game
cards.text: Animals "play" strategies shaped by evolution: hawks fight, doves share. A mix of both can be stable in a population.

cards.title: Splitting the bill
cards.text: When a group splits a restaurant bill equally, everyone is tempted to order more, since others share the cost. Everyone ends up paying more: a small tragedy of the commons.

quiz.q: In the prisoner's dilemma, what usually happens?
options: Both betray and are worse off

quiz.q: Which strategy did well in Axelrod's tournaments?

lessons.title: Codes and cryptography
lessons.summary: Secret messages from Caesar to your phone.

cards.title: The Caesar cipher
cards.text: Julius Caesar shifted each letter three places: A becomes D, B becomes E. Easy to use, and easy to break.

cards.title: Breaking codes with frequency
cards.text: In English, E is the most common letter, followed by T and A. Count letters in a coded message and you can guess the substitution. Al-Kindi described this in the 9th century.

cards.title: Vigenère
cards.text: The Vigenère cipher uses a keyword to shift each letter by a different amount, defeating simple frequency counts. It was called "the indecipherable cipher" for 300 years.

cards.title: Enigma
cards.text: Germany's Enigma machine used rotors to change the cipher with every key press. Polish mathematicians first cracked it; Alan Turing's team at Bletchley Park broke it at scale.

cards.title: Keys
cards.text: Modern encryption is public: the method is known, and security comes entirely from a secret key. A 128-bit key has trillions of times more combinations than there are grains of sand on Earth.

cards.title: Public-key cryptography
cards.text: Your phone uses two keys: a public one anyone can use to lock a message, and a private one only you have to unlock it. Invented in the 1970s.

cards.title: The padlock analogy
cards.text: Send someone an open padlock: they lock a box with it, and only you have the key. Nobody needed to share a secret beforehand.

cards.title: Hashes
cards.text: A hash turns any data into a fixed-length fingerprint. Change one letter and the hash changes completely. Websites store password hashes, not passwords.

cards.title: Strong passwords

items.r: four random words, plus a password manager

cards.text: Length beats complexity. Four random words are easier to remember and harder to crack than "P@ssw0rd1". Use a password manager and two-factor authentication.

cards.title: Quantum threat
cards.text: Large quantum computers could one day break today's public-key systems. New "post-quantum" algorithms were standardised in 2024 to prepare.

quiz.q: What breaks simple substitution ciphers?
quiz.explain: E is the most common letter in English.

quiz.q: In public-key cryptography, which key do you keep secret?

cards.title: Euclid
cards.text: Around 300 BCE Euclid wrote *Elements*, building geometry from a few basic axioms. It was used as a textbook for over 2,000 years.

cards.title: Archimedes
cards.text: Archimedes estimated π, worked out volumes of spheres, explained levers and buoyancy, and supposedly shouted "Eureka!" in his bath.

cards.title: Hypatia
cards.text: Hypatia of Alexandria (c. 360–415 CE) was a mathematician, astronomer and teacher, one of the first women in maths we know by name.

cards.title: Fibonacci
cards.text: Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, popularised Hindu-Arabic numerals in Europe in 1202 with his *Liber Abaci*, a book for merchants.

cards.title: Descartes and Fermat
cards.text: In the 1600s both linked algebra and geometry with coordinates. Fermat also left a famous "last theorem", unproved for 358 years.

cards.title: Newton and Leibniz
cards.text: Both invented calculus independently in the late 1600s and argued bitterly about who was first. We use Leibniz's notation today.

cards.title: Euler
cards.text: Leonhard Euler was the most prolific mathematician ever, writing over 800 papers even after going blind. His identity e^iπ + 1 = 0 links five key numbers.

cards.title: Gauss
cards.text: As a boy, Gauss supposedly summed 1 to 100 in seconds: pair 1+100, 2+99… into 50 pairs of 101, giving 5,050.

cards.title: Ada Lovelace
cards.text: In 1843 Ada Lovelace wrote what's considered the first computer program, for Babbage's Analytical Engine, and foresaw computers making music.

cards.title: Modern greats
cards.text: Emmy Noether linked symmetry and conservation laws; Ramanujan found startling formulas with little formal training; Maryam Mirzakhani was the first woman to win the Fields Medal, in 2014.

quiz.q: How did young Gauss sum 1 to 100?
Who wrote the first published computer program?

cards.title: Two big questions
cards.text: Calculus answers two questions: how fast is something changing right now (derivatives), and how much has built up over time (integrals).

cards.title: Instant speed
cards.text: Your car's speedometer shows speed at an instant, not an average. Calculus defines it by measuring over shorter and shorter time intervals.

cards.title: Slope of a curve
cards.text: A derivative is the slope of a curve at a point: zoom in far enough and any smooth curve looks like a straight line.

cards.title: Area under a curve
cards.text: An integral adds up tiny slices. On a speed–time graph, the area under the curve is the distance travelled.

cards.title: Opposites
cards.text: Differentiation and integration undo each other: the fundamental theorem of calculus. Distance → speed → acceleration, and back again.

cards.title: Maxima and minima
cards.text: Where a curve peaks or dips, its slope is zero. That's how engineers find the strongest beam or cheapest design.

cards.title: The biggest box
cards.text: Cut squares from a 30 cm card's corners and fold up a box. Calculus shows 5 cm squares give the largest volume: 2,000 cm³.

cards.title: Change everywhere
cards.text: Calculus models population growth, heating and cooling, interest, rocket trajectories and machine learning, which uses derivatives to adjust its weights.

cards.title: Limits
cards.text: Calculus rests on limits: what a value approaches as something gets very small. 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8… approaches 1, even though no step reaches it.

cards.title: Who invented it?
cards.text: Newton and Leibniz developed calculus independently in the 1660s–1680s, though Archimedes and others had used similar ideas centuries earlier.

quiz.q: On a speed–time graph, what does the area under the curve give?
At the top of a smooth curve, the slope is…
quiz.explain: Peaks and valleys have zero slope.

cards.title: Königsberg's bridges
cards.text: In 1736 Euler proved you couldn't walk across all seven bridges of Königsberg exactly once. To solve it, he reduced the city to dots and lines: graph theory was born.

cards.title: Nodes and edges
cards.text: A graph is a set of nodes (dots) joined by edges (lines). Cities and roads, people and friendships, web pages and links are all graphs.

cards.title: Euler's rule
cards.text: You can trace a network using every edge once only if zero or two nodes have an odd number of edges. Königsberg had four odd nodes.

cards.title: Shortest paths
cards.text: Your map app finds the fastest route with algorithms like Dijkstra's (1956), which explores outward from the start, always extending the shortest path found so far.

cards.title: The travelling salesman
cards.text: Find the shortest route visiting every city once. Easy for 5 cities, but the possibilities explode: 20 cities have over 60 quadrillion routes.

cards.title: Six degrees
cards.text: Stanley Milgram's 1967 experiment suggested any two Americans are linked by about six acquaintances. Facebook data later found an average of about 3.5 steps.

cards.title: Hubs
cards.text: In many networks a few hubs have huge numbers of links: major airports, popular websites, influencers. Attack the hubs and the network breaks.

cards.title: Four colours
cards.text: Any map can be coloured with just four colours so no neighbouring regions match. Proved in 1976, it was the first major proof that relied on a computer.

cards.title: PageRank

steps: Votes from important pages count more

cards.text: Google's original idea: a page is important if important pages link to it. It treats the web as a giant graph of votes.

cards.title: Epidemics on networks
cards.text: Diseases spread along contact networks. Vaccinating well-connected hubs, like healthcare workers, can protect far more people than random vaccination.

cards.title: Fermi problems
cards.text: Physicist Enrico Fermi loved questions like "how many piano tuners are in Chicago?" Break them into pieces you can guess, multiply, and you'll often be within a factor of a few.

cards.title: Petrol stations in Portugal
cards.text: About 10 million people, roughly 5 million cars, each filling up weekly: 5 million fills a week. If a station handles about 3,000 a week, that's around 1,700 stations; the real number is a few thousand.

cards.title: Orders of magnitude
cards.text: Often the power of 10 matters more than the exact value. Is it hundreds, thousands or millions? Get that right first.

cards.title: Useful anchors
cards.text: Memorise a few reference numbers and you can estimate almost anything.

cards.title: Round generously
cards.text: Round to numbers that are easy to multiply. 47 × 213 ≈ 50 × 200 = 10,000. The real answer is 10,011.

cards.title: Over and under cancel
cards.text: In multi-step estimates, rounding errors in different directions tend to cancel, so the final answer is often better than any single guess.

cards.title: Sanity checks
cards.text: Estimation catches mistakes. If a spreadsheet says a café uses 40 tonnes of coffee a day, a quick estimate shows something's wrong.

cards.title: Estimating crowds
cards.text: Count the people in a small area, then multiply by how many such areas the crowd covers. Police and organisers often disagree by a factor of two.

cards.title: How long is a billion seconds?
cards.text: A million seconds is about 11.5 days. A billion seconds is about 32 years. Big numbers are very different even if they sound similar.

cards.title: Confidence ranges
cards.text: Good estimators give ranges: "between 2,000 and 4,000". A range you're 90% sure about is more honest than a single precise-looking number.

quiz.q: How long is a billion seconds?
quiz.explain: A million seconds is about 11.5 days.

quiz.q: What is a Fermi problem?
options: A rough estimate built from simple guesses

cards.title: Arithmetic sequences
cards.text: Add the same number each time: 3, 7, 11, 15… (add 4). The nth term is easy to find: 4n − 1.

cards.title: Geometric sequences
cards.text: Multiply by the same number each time: 2, 6, 18, 54… (×3). They grow much faster than arithmetic sequences.

cards.title: Triangular numbers
cards.text: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15: the number of dots in growing triangles, like bowling pins. The nth is n(n + 1)/2.

cards.title: Fibonacci in nature
cards.text: Many sunflowers have 34 and 55 spirals; pine cones show 8 and 13. These Fibonacci numbers pack seeds efficiently.

cards.title: The golden ratio
cards.text: Divide each Fibonacci number by the one before and you approach 1.618…, the golden ratio φ.

cards.title: Pascal's triangle
cards.text: Each number is the sum of the two above it. The triangle hides counting numbers, triangular numbers, powers of 2 and probabilities of coin tosses.

cards.title: Primes resist patterns
cards.text: Primes thin out but never stop, and no simple formula produces them all. Predicting them is one of maths' deepest open problems.

cards.title: Tricky sequences
cards.text: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16… seems obvious, but cut a circle with lines between points and you get 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, then 31. Patterns need proof.

cards.title: Look-and-say
cards.text: 1, 11, 21, 1211, 111221… Each term describes the last aloud: "one 1", "two 1s", "one 2, one 1". A pattern based on words, not arithmetic.

cards.title: Find the rule
cards.text: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26… The gaps are 3, 5, 7, 9: odd numbers. The rule is n² + 1.

quiz.q: What comes next: 2, 6, 18, 54, …?

lessons.title: Measurement and units
lessons.summary: Metres, kilos and why they matter.

cards.title: The metric system
cards.text: Born in revolutionary France in the 1790s, the metric system uses powers of 10, so converting is just moving the decimal point. Portugal adopted it in 1852.

cards.title: Seven base units
cards.text: All measurements are built from seven SI base units. Since 2019, all are defined by fixed constants of nature, not physical objects.

cards.title: Goodbye, Le Grand K
cards.text: For 130 years the kilogram was a metal cylinder in a vault near Paris. In 2019 it was redefined using the Planck constant.

cards.title: Area and volume units
cards.text: 1 m² is 10,000 cm², not 100. 1 m³ is 1,000 litres. Units square and cube along with the lengths.

cards.title: Hectares
cards.text: A hectare is 100 m × 100 m = 10,000 m², about one and a half football pitches. Farms and forests are measured in hectares.

cards.title: Imperial units
cards.text: The UK and USA still use miles, pounds and Fahrenheit. Quick conversions: 1 mile ≈ 1.6 km, 1 kg ≈ 2.2 lb, 1 inch = 2.54 cm.

cards.title: The Mars Climate Orbiter
cards.text: In 1999 a NASA probe was lost at Mars because one team used pound-force and another newtons. The $125 million mistake was a units mix-up.

cards.title: Significant figures
cards.text: Precision should match the measurement. A room measured as 4.2 m doesn't have an area of 17.64 m² precisely; say about 17.6 m².

cards.title: Speed units
cards.text: Divide km/h by 3.6 for metres per second. 120 km/h is about 33 m/s: a car covers a football pitch every three seconds.

cards.title: Energy units
cards.text: A kilowatt-hour runs a 1,000 W heater for an hour. A food Calorie is 1,000 calories, about 4.2 kJ. A hot shower uses about 2–3 kWh.

options: A mix-up of imperial and metric units

cards.title: The Tower of Hanoi
cards.text: Move a stack of discs to another peg, one at a time, never placing a bigger disc on a smaller one. With n discs it takes 2ⁿ − 1 moves.

cards.title: Missing square

items.r: The edges are slightly bent: the shapes aren't equal

cards.text: Rearranging four pieces of a triangle seems to create a hole. The trick: the "hypotenuses" aren't straight lines, so the shapes differ slightly.

cards.title: The handshake problem
cards.text: If 10 people all shake hands once, how many handshakes? Each shakes 9 hands, but each handshake involves two: 10 × 9 ÷ 2 = 45.

cards.title: Pigeonhole principle

steps: At least one box has two

cards.text: If you put 13 socks into 12 drawers, at least one drawer gets two. Simple but powerful: in Lisbon, at least two people have exactly the same number of hairs on their head.

cards.title: The 0.999… puzzle
cards.text: 0.999… repeating forever equals exactly 1. One proof: 1/3 = 0.333…, so 3 × 1/3 = 0.999… = 1.

cards.title: Hilbert's hotel
cards.text: A hotel with infinitely many rooms is full. A new guest arrives: move everyone from room n to room n + 1, and room 1 is free. Infinity behaves strangely.

cards.title: Truth tellers and liars
cards.text: On an island, knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. Ask either "what would the other say?" and you can reverse the answer to find the truth.

cards.title: Sudoku is logic
cards.text: Sudoku needs no arithmetic, only logic: each row, column and box contains 1 to 9 once. A well-made puzzle has exactly one solution.

cards.title: The Seven Bridges today
cards.text: Euler's idea is used in garbage collection and postal routes: planning paths that cover every street once with as little doubling back as possible.

cards.title: The wolf, goat and cabbage, solved
cards.text: The key insight was taking something back. Many puzzles need a step that seems to go backwards, a lesson for real problem-solving too.
